comments_structured.author: etsaur
comments_structured.text: Logging and raising visibility Note, this patch has NOT been up-streamed. (we're around 6.11-rc5 as of this message) Concern for missing this patch is that it only hurts Intel.  ie. AMD and ARM are unlikely affected. This is because of the way Intel report RP CXL.CM errors.   Birchstream (CXL 2.0) and beyond is reporting CXL.CM errors in a fashion described for CXL 1.1. Basically RP CXL.CM errors are reported by an associated RCEC. Summary of the story without this patch is: (by Dan Williams) """ However, in the meantime it does mean that AMD can say "error handling works out-of-the-box starting with CXL 2.0 platforms, our CXL 1.1 platforms still need some Linux hacks." While Intel says "we need Linux hacks for CXL 1.1 and 2.0" """

articles.full_text:
TITLE: [RAS_DM][CXL] CXL.MEM correctable errors OS error handling is incomplete in OSFM

DESCRIPTION:
This issue was seen in previously in EGS platforms: [EMR][SPR][CXL] CXL.MEM error handling and signaling incomplete in OS First Mode with CXL 1.0 The problem is the following: When a CXL.MEM error happens in OSFM the error handler only attends the error in the RCEC keeping the error logged in the CXL AER register when this register is not cleared a CXL Root Port is not sending new AER messages to IEH unless the previous error is cleared. The handling is matching the specification: https://docs.intel.com/documents/iparch/cxlcm/HAS/Gen4/features/IPCXL-223/IPCXL_223_FHAS.html#reliability-availability-and-serviceability-ras-4 Error Flow DP A .io logs errors in local AER Ext Cap (in RCRB) DP A .cache & .mem logs errors in Mem Space registers DP A .cache, .mem, or .io sends PCIe AER msg with .io block Src Port ID on SB to Sat IEH B Sat IEH B logs received PCIe AER msg in single Local Error register (same Src Port ID) Sat IEH B logs UIE/CIE in RCEC Sat IEH B logs source (RCEC) in Global Error Sat IEH B generates PCIe Error msg on SB to Gbl IEH With own ReqID and strapped Bitmap OS Error Handling Inspect and handle RCEC AER FW Error Handling Inspect Gbl IEH Global Error Inspect Sat IEH Global Error Inspect RCEC AER and Local Error Inspect DP AER & handle Mem (or Cache, IO) errors But this flow has to be enhanced to complete a successful error handling in the CXL root port.

I noticed the subject line changed... Technically OSFM doesn't handle uncorrectable errors either. RCEC sees a UIE, but OS doesn't go the CXL.CM and read uncorrectable error status register either. It's just less obvious because the OS usually doesn't survive. Need to study the not reporting issue.  Loosing future errors is acceptable as seen by. https://hsdes.intel.com/appstore/article/#/22016951635 If we had a full OSFM handling or even FFM, we could have a race condition where. - Read RCEC (UIE/CIE) - Read CXL.CM - Clear CXL.CM <-- New CXL.CM error comes in (Will a new interrupt be triggered, because RCEC UIE/CIE hasn't been cleared yet?) - Clear RCEC  Results will be - RCEC Clear <== even if a new interrupt was sent, normal code would stop at RCEC because UIE/CIE = 0. - CXL.CM has error <== prevents future errors from interrupting? We would need an algorithm like - Read RCEC (UIE/CIE) - Clear RCEC  - Read CXL.CM - Clear CXL.CM <-- New CXL.CM error comes in (will trigger new UIE/CIE and hopefully trigger an interrupt) Heavily tested and documented. Otherwise we end up with 22016951635 again.

raw.description:
This issue was seen in previously in EGS platforms: [EMR][SPR][CXL] CXL.MEM error handling and signaling incomplete in OS First Mode with CXL 1.0


The problem is the following:

When a CXL.MEM error happens in OSFM the error handler only attends the error in the RCEC keeping the error logged in the CXL AER register when this register is not cleared a CXL Root Port is not sending new AER messages to IEH unless the previous error is cleared.


The handling is matching the specification:

https://docs.intel.com/documents/iparch/cxlcm/HAS/Gen4/features/IPCXL-223/IPCXL_223_FHAS.html#reliability-availability-and-serviceability-ras-4


Error Flow

  • DPA .io logs errors in local AER Ext Cap (in RCRB)
  • DPA .cache & .mem logs errors in Mem Space registers
  • DPA .cache, .mem, or .io sends PCIe AER msg with .io block Src Port ID on SB to Sat IEHB
  • Sat IEHB logs received PCIe AER msg in single Local Error register (same Src Port ID)
  • Sat IEHB logs UIE/CIE in RCEC
  • Sat IEHB logs source (RCEC) in Global Error
  • Sat IEHB generates PCIe Error msg on SB to Gbl IEH
    • With own ReqID and strapped Bitmap

OS Error Handling

  • Inspect and handle RCEC AER

FW Error Handling

  • Inspect Gbl IEH Global Error
  • Inspect Sat IEH Global Error
  • Inspect RCEC AER and Local Error
  • Inspect DP AER & handle Mem (or Cache, IO) errors


But this flow has to be enhanced to complete a successful error handling in the CXL root port.

++++1469755059 etsaur
I noticed the subject line changed... Technically OSFM doesn't handle uncorrectable errors either. RCEC sees a UIE, but OS doesn't go the CXL.CM and read uncorrectable error status register either. It's just less obvious because the OS usually doesn't survive. Need to study the not reporting issue.  Loosing future errors is acceptable as seen by. https://hsdes.intel.com/appstore/article/#/22016951635 If we had a full OSFM handling or even FFM, we could have a race condition where. - Read RCEC (UIE/CIE) - Read CXL.CM - Clear CXL.CM <-- New CXL.CM error comes in (Will a new interrupt be triggered, because RCEC UIE/CIE hasn't been cleared yet?) - Clear RCEC  Results will be - RCEC Clear <== even if a new interrupt was sent, normal code would stop at RCEC because UIE/CIE = 0. - CXL.CM has error <== prevents future errors from interrupting? We would need an algorithm like - Read RCEC (UIE/CIE) - Clear RCEC  - Read CXL.CM - Clear CXL.CM <-- New CXL.CM error comes in (will trigger new UIE/CIE and hopefully trigger an interrupt) Heavily tested and documented. Otherwise we end up with 22016951635 again.

articles.title: [RAS][CXL][Accelerators] RCEC uncorrectable fatal errors are not triggering the platform reset in OSFM
articles.description: This problem was previously seen in EGS platforms [EMR][SPR][CXL] CXL.MEM fatal error is neither logging IOMCA nor taking fatal actions in OS First Mode The error is reported and signaled as fatal by the OS: [335053.375407] pcieport 0000:27:00.4: AER: Uncorrected (Fatal) error received: 0000:27:00.4 [335053.376093] pcieport 0000:27:00.4: PCIe Bus Error: severity=Uncorrected (Fatal), type=Transaction Layer, (Receiver ID) [335053.376193] pcieport 0000:27:00.4: device [8086:0b23] error status/mask=00400000/00180020 [335053.376276] pcieport 0000:27:00.4: [22] UncorrIntErr (First) [335053.376635] pcieport 0000:27:00.4: AER: not reset (no FLR support: -25) [335053.376651] pcieport 0000:27:00.4: AER: subordinate device reset failed [335053.379067] pcieport 0000:27:00.4: AER: device recovery failed But no reset is performed. From last debug comment in the old HSD the error scalation in the IEH is what is generating this problem.
comments:
Looking at the kernel documentation: 8.3.2.4. Non-correctable (non-fatal and fatal) errors¶ If an error message indicates a non-fatal error, performing link reset at upstream is not required. The AER driver calls error_detected(dev, pci_channel_io_normal) to all drivers associated within a hierarchy in question. for example: EndPoint DownstreamPort B UpstreamPort A RootPort
 If Upstream port A captures an AER error, the hierarchy consists of Downstream port B and EndPoint. A driver may return PCI_ERS_RESULT_CAN_RECOVER, PCI_ERS_RESULT_DISCONNECT, or PCI_ERS_RESULT_NEED_RESET, depending on whether it can recover or the AER driver calls mmio_enabled as next. If an error message indicates a fatal error, kernel will broadcast error_detected(dev, pci_channel_io_frozen) to all drivers within a hierarchy in question. Then, performing link reset at upstream is necessary. As different kinds of devices might use different approaches to reset link, AER port service driver is required to provide the function to reset link via callback parameter of pcie_do_recovery() function. If reset_link is not NULL, recovery function will use it to reset the link. If error_detected returns PCI_ERS_RESULT_CAN_RECOVER and reset_link returns PCI_ERS_RESULT_RECOVERED, the error handling goes to mmio_enabled. Looks like the result is the expected by the kernel. So the suspicion is still the error scalation in IEH.

Ok my hypothesis was verified: I changed the Satellite IEH configuration to send system error messages to global IEH. In [39]: sv.socket0.io0.uncore.satieh.satieh4.rootctl Out[39]: 0x8 In [40]: sv.socket0.io0.uncore.satieh.satieh4.rootctl=0xf In [41]: sv.socket0.io0.uncore.satieh.satieh4.rootctl Out[41]: 0xf After this change the IOMCA reporting is seen: jf53nor15an0104 login: [ 1094.398670] mce: [Hardware Error]: CPU 0: Machine Check Exception: 5 Bank 4: ba00000000000e0b [ 1094.408304] mce: [Hardware Error]: RIP !INEXACT! 33: [ 1094.415785] mce: [Hardware Error]: TSC 28dcbc16951 MISC 27040000 [ 1094.422675] mce: [Hardware Error]: PROCESSOR 0:a06d0 TIME 1685416812 SOCKET 0 APIC 0 microcode 88000038 [ 1094.433272] mce: [Hardware Error]: Run the above through 'mcelog --ascii' [ 1094.490762] mce: [Hardware Error]: Machine check: Processor context corrupt [ 1094.498645] Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal machine check [ 1094.524900] Kernel Offset: 0x2b000000 from 0xffffffff81000000 (relocation range: 0xffffffff80000000-0xffffffffbfffffff) [ 1094.863117] ******************************************************************************************** [ 1094.863117] * WARNING: Project Intel Next sources and binaries include Intel Confidential information. * [ 1094.863117] *          For use by Intel Employees only; do not distribute externally.                  * [ 1094.863117] ******************************************************************************************** [ 1094.905701] Rebooting in 999999 seconds..

Summary: Due to the current Satellite IEH configuration the Global IEH is unaware of the fatal errors when in OSFM and in consequence the platform reset is not triggered. This configuration could also affect PCIe errors but as DPC is enabled by default when in OSFM I think this error was masked.
@Garcia Rodriguez, Diego - What ingredient would make this change in error propagation?  Is it BIOS?

Hi @Jeppesen, Mark C BIOS can make the change in this flow. The problem here is that BIOS is configuring correctly the IEH Satellite because in OSFM the errors has to signal the error using interrupts (MSI/INTx) to get the handling from OS, something that is missing in this flow is that to get the extra error handling that Global IEH provides (ERR Pins, IOMCA) we need to notify it with an ERRMSG. So as seen in previous comments was corroborated that by configuring Satellite IEH we can complete the Fatal Flow, But this configuration is like a mix between FFM and OSFM. My plan was to start a thread with Arch but I am waiting for a resolution for https://hsdes.intel.com/appstore/article/#/14019463740 first to avoid to much noise. Do you have another idea on how can we address this situation?
Thanks Diego. Seems like trying to get this figured out with architecture is the right path. And having consistency amongst the platforms is the right thing to do.

We may treat OS first mode as part of CLX.mem error isolation (DPC) feature, which is not POR on GNR? It includes both FFM and OS first mode.  1. FFM: BIOS added one knobs to disable CXL.mem error isolation by default. Currently only CXL.io eDPC is supported like PCIe 2. OS First mode: if it's not POR like FFM,  OS does not have capability to recover it, not like PCIe which signal to OS via MSI directly without IEH involvement and get recovered from OS.    Should we remove the config?  CXL.Mem Error Isolation support https://hsdes.intel.com/appstore/article/#/22013133657 Optional OS recovery actions with FFM enabled or disabled
Thanks for your proposal @Li, Jun J but this is just masking the problem in the fatal flow in OSFM. We need to define a flow without the error isolation.

Thanks, Diego! I understand. Actually It's similar to RCiEP devices which reports to RCEC (Satellite IEH) like CXL.mem/Cache.  For example: DSA fatal error injection under OS first mode, OS cannot recover as below and system don't reboot, DSAx device will be inaccessible due to unsupported failed OS recovery.  idxd 0000:00:01.0: AER: PCIe Bus Error: severity=Uncorrected (Fatal), type=Inaccessible, (Unregistered Agent ID) Note: The good thing is DMR + CXL 3.0 do not need to report to RCEC, and CXL.mem error isolation will be POR as well.

@Garcia Rodriguez, Diego  - Is this a duplicate of 14019463740 - [RAS][CXL] CXL.MEM correctable errors OS error handling is incomplete in OSFM (intel.com) or is that just a gate to further debug on this sighting.  If duplicate can we reject one?

So it turns out there are multiple scenarios where Linux software can learn of a CXL fatal event but takes no preemptive reset action. In addition to IOMCA AER fatal there are also CXL Error isolation events. I did a write-up of the challenges of the CXL Error isolation architecture around the challenges of surprise losing a memory device at runtime. One takeaway there is that the eventual reset due to memory access fatal errors is the default expectation and likely the best software can do relative to the challenges to resetting a CXL memory device in active use. Linux is simply not prepared for massive memory failure events. I see a similar challenge with trying to handle AER fatal. In general, as long as the system is still otherwise running it should continue to run. If the CXL device is dead then it *may* trigger knock-on effects for CPU fatal events result in resets when the CPU is not recoverable, but as long as the CPU has not experienced a fatal event why should software preemptively take down the whole system on a single AER device fatal event?

Let's discuss these points at the RAS WG this week. For AER fatal, since the fundamentals of PCIe protocol may be compromised, the system really aught to go down.  There is a chance of unmitigated corruption that may occur.  Panic'ing to stem the unmitigated corruption is not the best solution, but doing nothing is worse IMO.  ERRPIN2 to DPC or RESET is better and taking a long time to panic. In either case there is a difference in behavior between FFM and OSFM that I feel we need to resolved.  For instance that may mean forwarding PCIe GHES records to the PCIe subsystem, vs letting the GHES subsystem deciding on weather to panic before fowarding.  That way we can eliminate any potential split personality behaviors in the future.  Huge change in behavior that may not make folks happy.  Or  have BIOS not send PCIe Fatal with a GHES Fatal severity.

Short summary of the RAS WG. Not doing anything does not seem right.  Currently system neither panics nor does it attempt an FLR, which wouldn't have helped CXL.mem errors. The inconsistency between FFM and OSFM is also not right. Following the motto, containment first as the big hammer when seeing a fatal error.  Which will at least bring OSFM and FFM in line with each other. Then work on recovery mechanism. Example future work/study, currently FFM panics on the GHES CPER PCIe based on the CPER severity.  It's panic'ing the system, but not for the right reasons.  It should forward the error to PCIe/CXL subsystem and let the PCIe/CXL decide on weather to panic the system. Example future work/study, instead of just reacting to the fact that there was a fatal error, examine what caused the error.  If the data is poisoned, then there may not be a need to panic as the poison, if consumed will result in some sort of MCE.

Looking at the kernel documentation: 8.3.2.4. Non-correctable (non-fatal and fatal) errors¶ If an error message indicates a non-fatal error, performing link reset at upstream is not required. The AER driver calls error_detected(dev, pci_channel_io_normal) to all drivers associated within a hierarchy in question. for example: EndPoint DownstreamPort B UpstreamPort A RootPort
 If Upstream port A captures an AER error, the hierarchy consists of Downstream port B and EndPoint. A driver may return PCI_ERS_RESULT_CAN_RECOVER, PCI_ERS_RESULT_DISCONNECT, or PCI_ERS_RESULT_NEED_RESET, depending on whether it can recover or the AER driver calls mmio_enabled as next. If an error message indicates a fatal error, kernel will broadcast error_detected(dev, pci_channel_io_frozen) to all drivers within a hierarchy in question. Then, performing link reset at upstream is necessary. As different kinds of devices might use different approaches to reset link, AER port service driver is required to provide the function to reset link via callback parameter of pcie_do_recovery() function. If reset_link is not NULL, recovery function will use it to reset the link. If error_detected returns PCI_ERS_RESULT_CAN_RECOVER and reset_link returns PCI_ERS_RESULT_RECOVERED, the error handling goes to mmio_enabled. Looks like the result is the expected by the kernel. So the suspicion is still the error scalation in IEH.

comments_structured.author: dwillia2
comments_structured.text: So it turns out there are multiple scenarios where Linux software can learn of a CXL fatal event but takes no preemptive reset action. In addition to IOMCA AER fatal there are also CXL Error isolation events. I did a write-up of the challenges of the CXL Error isolation architecture around the challenges of surprise losing a memory device at runtime. One takeaway there is that the eventual reset due to memory access fatal errors is the default expectation and likely the best software can do relative to the challenges to resetting a CXL memory device in active use. Linux is simply not prepared for massive memory failure events. I see a similar challenge with trying to handle AER fatal. In general, as long as the system is still otherwise running it should continue to run. If the CXL device is dead then it *may* trigger knock-on effects for CPU fatal events result in resets when the CPU is not recoverable, but as long as the CPU has not experienced a fatal event why should software preemptively take down the whole system on a single AER device fatal event?

comments_structured.author: etsaur
comments_structured.text: Let's discuss these points at the RAS WG this week. For AER fatal, since the fundamentals of PCIe protocol may be compromised, the system really aught to go down.  There is a chance of unmitigated corruption that may occur.  Panic'ing to stem the unmitigated corruption is not the best solution, but doing nothing is worse IMO.  ERRPIN2 to DPC or RESET is better and taking a long time to panic. In either case there is a difference in behavior between FFM and OSFM that I feel we need to resolved.  For instance that may mean forwarding PCIe GHES records to the PCIe subsystem, vs letting the GHES subsystem deciding on weather to panic before fowarding.  That way we can eliminate any potential split personality behaviors in the future.  Huge change in behavior that may not make folks happy.  Or  have BIOS not send PCIe Fatal with a GHES Fatal severity.

comments_structured.text: Short summary of the RAS WG. Not doing anything does not seem right.  Currently system neither panics nor does it attempt an FLR, which wouldn't have helped CXL.mem errors. The inconsistency between FFM and OSFM is also not right. Following the motto, containment first as the big hammer when seeing a fatal error.  Which will at least bring OSFM and FFM in line with each other. Then work on recovery mechanism. Example future work/study, currently FFM panics on the GHES CPER PCIe based on the CPER severity.  It's panic'ing the system, but not for the right reasons.  It should forward the error to PCIe/CXL subsystem and let the PCIe/CXL decide on weather to panic the system. Example future work/study, instead of just reacting to the fact that there was a fatal error, examine what caused the error.  If the data is poisoned, then there may not be a need to panic as the poison, if consumed will result in some sort of MCE.

articles.full_text:
TITLE: [RAS][CXL][Accelerators] RCEC uncorrectable fatal errors are not triggering the platform reset in OSFM

DESCRIPTION:
This problem was previously seen in EGS platforms [EMR][SPR][CXL] CXL.MEM fatal error is neither logging IOMCA nor taking fatal actions in OS First Mode The error is reported and signaled as fatal by the OS: [335053.375407] pcieport 0000:27:00.4: AER: Uncorrected (Fatal) error received: 0000:27:00.4 [335053.376093] pcieport 0000:27:00.4: PCIe Bus Error: severity=Uncorrected (Fatal), type=Transaction Layer, (Receiver ID) [335053.376193] pcieport 0000:27:00.4: device [8086:0b23] error status/mask=00400000/00180020 [335053.376276] pcieport 0000:27:00.4: [22] UncorrIntErr (First) [335053.376635] pcieport 0000:27:00.4: AER: not reset (no FLR support: -25) [335053.376651] pcieport 0000:27:00.4: AER: subordinate device reset failed [335053.379067] pcieport 0000:27:00.4: AER: device recovery failed But no reset is performed. From last debug comment in the old HSD the error scalation in the IEH is what is generating this problem.

COMMENTS:
Looking at the kernel documentation: 8.3.2.4. Non-correctable (non-fatal and fatal) errors¶ If an error message indicates a non-fatal error, performing link reset at upstream is not required. The AER driver calls error_detected(dev, pci_channel_io_normal) to all drivers associated within a hierarchy in question. for example: EndPoint DownstreamPort B UpstreamPort A RootPort
 If Upstream port A captures an AER error, the hierarchy consists of Downstream port B and EndPoint. A driver may return PCI_ERS_RESULT_CAN_RECOVER, PCI_ERS_RESULT_DISCONNECT, or PCI_ERS_RESULT_NEED_RESET, depending on whether it can recover or the AER driver calls mmio_enabled as next. If an error message indicates a fatal error, kernel will broadcast error_detected(dev, pci_channel_io_frozen) to all drivers within a hierarchy in question. Then, performing link reset at upstream is necessary. As different kinds of devices might use different approaches to reset link, AER port service driver is required to provide the function to reset link via callback parameter of pcie_do_recovery() function. If reset_link is not NULL, recovery function will use it to reset the link. If error_detected returns PCI_ERS_RESULT_CAN_RECOVER and reset_link returns PCI_ERS_RESULT_RECOVERED, the error handling goes to mmio_enabled. Looks like the result is the expected by the kernel. In addition to IOMCA AER fatal there are also CXL Error isolation events. I did a write-up of the challenges of the CXL Error isolation architecture around the challenges of surprise losing a memory device at runtime. One takeaway there is that the eventual reset due to memory access fatal errors is the default expectation and likely the best software can do relative to the challenges to resetting a CXL memory device in active use. Linux is simply not prepared for massive memory failure events. I see a similar challenge with trying to handle AER fatal. In general, as long as the system is still otherwise running it should continue to run. If the CXL device is dead then it *may* trigger knock-on effects for CPU fatal events result in resets when the CPU is not recoverable, but as long as the CPU has not experienced a fatal event why should software preemptively take down the whole system on a single AER device fatal event?
Let's discuss these points at the RAS WG this week. For AER fatal, since the fundamentals of PCIe protocol may be compromised, the system really aught to go down.  There is a chance of unmitigated corruption that may occur.  Panic'ing to stem the unmitigated corruption is not the best solution, but doing nothing is worse IMO.  ERRPIN2 to DPC or RESET is better and taking a long time to panic. In either case there is a difference in behavior between FFM and OSFM that I feel we need to resolved.  For instance that may mean forwarding PCIe GHES records to the PCIe subsystem, vs letting the GHES subsystem deciding on weather to panic before fowarding.  That way we can eliminate any potential split personality behaviors in the future.  Huge change in behavior that may not make folks happy.  Or  have BIOS not send PCIe Fatal with a GHES Fatal severity.

Short summary of the RAS WG. Not doing anything does not seem right.  Currently system neither panics nor does it attempt an FLR, which wouldn't have helped CXL.mem errors. The inconsistency between FFM and OSFM is also not right. Following the motto, containment first as the big hammer when seeing a fatal error.  Which will at least bring OSFM and FFM in line with each other. Then work on recovery mechanism. Example future work/study, currently FFM panics on the GHES CPER PCIe based on the CPER severity.  It's panic'ing the system, but not for the right reasons.  It should forward the error to PCIe/CXL subsystem and let the PCIe/CXL decide on weather to panic the system. Example future work/study, instead of just reacting to the fact that there was a fatal error, examine what caused the error.  If the data is poisoned, then there may not be a need to panic as the poison, if consumed will result in some sort of MCE.

++++1469752201 diegog3
Looking at the kernel documentation: 8.3.2.4. Non-correctable (non-fatal and fatal) errors¶ If an error message indicates a non-fatal error, performing link reset at upstream is not required. The AER driver calls error_detected(dev, pci_channel_io_normal) to all drivers associated within a hierarchy in question. for example: EndPoint<==>DownstreamPort B<==>UpstreamPort A<==>RootPort
 If Upstream port A captures an AER error, the hierarchy consists of Downstream port B and EndPoint. A driver may return PCI_ERS_RESULT_CAN_RECOVER, PCI_ERS_RESULT_DISCONNECT, or PCI_ERS_RESULT_NEED_RESET, depending on whether it can recover or the AER driver calls mmio_enabled as next. If an error message indicates a fatal error, kernel will broadcast error_detected(dev, pci_channel_io_frozen) to all drivers within a hierarchy in question. Then, performing link reset at upstream is necessary. As different kinds of devices might use different approaches to reset link, AER port service driver is required to provide the function to reset link via callback parameter of pcie_do_recovery() function. If reset_link is not NULL, recovery function will use it to reset the link. If error_detected returns PCI_ERS_RESULT_CAN_RECOVER and reset_link returns PCI_ERS_RESULT_RECOVERED, the error handling goes to mmio_enabled. Looks like the result is the expected by the kernel. So the suspicion is still the error scalation in IEH.

So it turns out there are multiple scenarios where Linux software can learn of a CXL fatal event but takes no preemptive reset action. In addition to IOMCA AER fatal there are also CXL Error isolation events. I did a write-up of the challenges of the CXL Error isolation architecture around the challenges of surprise losing a memory device at runtime. One takeaway there is that the eventual reset due to memory access fatal errors is the default expectation and likely the best software can do relative to the challenges to resetting a CXL memory device in active use. Linux is simply not prepared for massive memory failure events. I see a similar challenge with trying to handle AER fatal. In general, as long as the system is still otherwise running it should continue to run. If the CXL device is dead then it *may* trigger knock-on effects for CPU fatal events result in resets when the CPU is not recoverable, but as long as the CPU has not experienced a fatal event why should software preemptively take down the whole system on a single AER device fatal event?

TITLE: [GNR][8S][: Windows Server 2022/2025 OS Installation Fails on Systems with VMD Enabled and RAID Configuration

DESCRIPTION:
Windows Server 2022/2025 OS Installation Fails on Systems with VMD Enabled and RAID Configuration Configuration: Socket System Stepping QDF DIMMs Storage SP-8S fl31ca105hn0501.amr.corp.intel.com B3 Q642 (Cores 80) 8+0 Micron Technology Socket 3: PE4 and PE5 Samsung NVMe U.2 SSDs via HSBP Bios BHSDCRB1.IPC.3544.P29.2412180234 Bmc bhs-24.40-2-gd4e1fe-6fddef2 Cpld 0.36 VROC 9.1.0.1449 Test Steps: ========= Scenario1: 1. Go to BIOS and enable Enable VMD on storage devices and reboot the system. 2. Go to BIOS and create RAID1 volume on 2 storage devices. 3. Install Windows OS by providing VROC F6 drivers. articles.title: [GNR SP 8S][BKC][8S][WHQL][PC] USB Exposed Port System Test fails showing too many USB ports
articles.description: [GNR-SP 8S] WHQL test, USB Exposed Port Test failing Background: This test expects all physically accessible USB3 ports to be plugged into a USB Hub. Part of the test is verifying the expected ports versus the actual ports, that is what is failing here. Failure: The test says that far more USB3 ports are expected (13 USB 3.0 ports) than are physically available (1 USB 3.0 port on each board). When plugging in a USB device to the actual physically available USB 3.0 port on each board, USBview shows that each USB 3.0 port is Port 3, Companion port 7. Screenshot of USBview showing the physical port on each board. Port 3, Companion port 7.
comments: There are 4 USB3.0 ports and 4 USB2.0 ports on GNR SP 8S system. (Each DC SCM have 1 USB3.0 port + 1 USB2.0 port and 8S system have 4 DC SCM.).(See the snapshot at below.) So the "13 exposed USB3.0 ports" should not be correct.  @Morton, Jessica  Do we have any USB hub connected in this failed system? Which windows chipset driver is installed? (14023023327 - Ingredient Versions - OneBKC  Chipset - 10.1.19928.8615-PUBLIC-SERVER - this is the driver in 8S BKC PC release)
No, there is no external USB hub connected the failing system. I have installed the  Chipset - 10.1.19928.8615-PUBLIC-SERVER

We have some findings on another 8S system. There are 13 USB3.0 ports ("Connectable" and "user visible") on 8S system: 4 USB 3.0 ports on USB xHCI Compliant Host Controller (BDF = 153.0.0) 4 USB 3.0 ports on USB xHCI Compliant Host Controller (BDF = 280.0.0) 4 USB 3.0 ports on USB xHCI Compliant Host Controller (BDF = 409.0.0) 1 USB 3.0 ports on USB xHCI Compliant Host Controller (BDF = 27.0.0) and the USB port routing of these USB controllers with BDF 153.0.0/280.0.0/409.0.0 are not following the design.

@Li, Fei@Feng, Ning  please help look at this issue. May impact the WHQL cert.

Have aligned with @Feng, Ning on how to scale the ACPI SSDT table to 2S/4S/8S configs in BIOS design and how to verify it under Windows without HLK tool.  @Feng, Ning will try to submit the initial PR to fix it.

TITLE: [GNR SP 8S][BKC][8S][WHQL][PC] USB Exposed Port System Test fails showing too many USB ports

DESCRIPTION:
[GNR-SP 8S] WHQL test, USB Exposed Port Test failing Background: This test expects all physically accessible USB3 ports to be plugged into a USB Hub. Part of the test is verifying the expected ports versus the actual ports, that is what is failing here. Failure: The test says that far more USB3 ports are expected (13 USB 3.0 ports) than are physically available (1 USB 3.0 port on each board). When plugging in a USB device to the actual physically available USB 3.0 port on each board, USBview shows that each USB 3.0 port is Port 3, Companion port 7. Screenshot of USBview showing the physical port on each board. Port 3, Companion port 7.

COMMENTS:
There are 4 USB3.0 ports and 4 USB2.0 ports on GNR SP 8S system. (Each DC SCM have 1 USB3.0 port + 1 USB2.0 port and 8S system have 4 DC SCM.).(See the snapshot at below.) So the "13 exposed USB3.0 ports" should not be correct.  @Morton, Jessica  Do we have any USB hub connected in this failed system? Which windows chipset driver is installed? (14023023327 - Ingredient Versions - OneBKC  Chipset - 10.1.19928.8615-PUBLIC-SERVER - this is the driver in 8S BKC PC release)
No, there is no external USB hub connected the failing system. I have installed the  Chipset - 10.1.19928.8615-PUBLIC-SERVER
We have some findings on another 8S system. There are 13 USB3.0 ports ("Connectable" and "user visible") on 8S system: 4 USB 3.0 ports on USB xHCI Compliant Host Controller (BDF = 153.0.0) 4 USB 3.0 ports on USB xHCI Compliant Host Controller (BDF = 280.0.0) 4 USB 3.0 ports on USB xHCI Compliant Host Controller (BDF = 409.0.0) 1 USB 3.0 ports on USB xHCI Compliant Host Controller (BDF = 27.0.0) and the USB port routing of these USB controllers with BDF 153.0.0/280.0.0/409.0.0 are not following the design.
This is the USB Port Routing by design: /* DC-SCM xHCI Controller (Renesas Technology Corp. uPD720201) USB Port Routing:   PortLogicNum   PortPhysicalNum   Routed To ------------   --------------- 'A' connector            Method (_PLD) { Return (GPLD(0, 0)) } // Not User Visible          }        }    } } It seems that USB port routing Map defined in BIOS doesn't work well on GNR 8S  - need articles.title: RTC inverse topology- RTC Date/Time Retention Lost During Cold/warm Reset Cycling, RTC Reverts to Default Timestamp (1998-01-01)
articles.description: During cold-reset cycling, the RTC maintains correct time through several iterations. Following next iteration, RTC reads become invalid, and upon recovery the RTC reports a default timestamp of 1998-01-01 instead of preserving the programmed date/time. The RTC continues counting after recovery, indicating loss of retained RTC state rather than oscillator stoppage. RTC initialized and verified correctly before reset testing. I²C trace shows the NCT3018Y RTC ( 0x6F ) programmed with a valid timestamp ( 2026-08-26 16:40:00 ) and successfully read back with matching values. RTC did not freeze after failure. Once the RTC recovered to 1998-01-01 , seconds and minutes continued advancing normally, indicating the oscillator and I²C interface remained operational.

TITLE: RTC inverse topology- RTC Date/Time Retention Lost During Cold/warm Reset Cycling, RTC Reverts to Default Timestamp (1998-01-01)

DESCRIPTION:
During cold-reset cycling, the RTC maintains correct time through several iterations. Following next iteration, RTC reads become invalid, and upon recovery the RTC reports a default timestamp of 1998-01-01 instead of preserving the programmed date/time. The RTC continues counting after recovery, indicating loss of retained RTC state rather than oscillator stoppage. RTC initialized and verified correctly before reset testing. I²C trace shows the NCT3018Y RTC ( 0x6F ) programmed with a valid timestamp ( 2026-08-26 16:40:00 ) and successfully read back with matching values. RTC did not freeze after failure. Once the RTC recovered to 1998-01-01 , seconds and minutes continued advancing normally, indicating the oscillator and I²C interface remained operational.

raw.description:
During cold-reset cycling, the RTC maintains correct time through several iterations. Following next iteration, RTC reads become invalid, and upon recovery the RTC reports a default timestamp of 1998-01-01 instead of preserving the programmed date/time. The RTC continues counting after recovery, indicating loss of retained RTC state rather than oscillator stoppage. 

RTC initialized and verified correctly before reset testing. I²C trace shows the NCT3018Y RTC (0x6F) programmed with a valid timestamp (2026-08-26 16:40:00) and successfully read back with matching values.

RTC did not freeze after failure. Once the RTC recovered to 1998-01-01, seconds and minutes continued advancing normally, indicating the oscillator and I²C interface remained operational.

I doubled checked all the log, but the regression observation from my side is the same. This signature appeared latest from 24/12/04, the IFWI and os at that time is 3544.P25+6.6.31.1.45. From the reproduction rate level, it is unlikely to be the case the issue existed but we did not catch that. Since you mentioned the kernel is the same as 6.6.29, I would like to confirm if other factors might cause this issue. Around the beginning of 24/12, we upgraded the CPU to QS sample and we also upgraded the IFWI . I have few observations: 1. The issue only occurs in 8S, not 2S/4S 2. None of 8S HCC QS systems hit this issue 3. One of my 8S HCC systems had never hit the issue, then it was upgraded to the QS sample (1280 cores) last week. The issue occurred after the CPU was upgraded. 4. One of my 8S QS systems with 1152 cores hit the issue, then it was upgraded to the QS sample with 1024 cores. The issue was gone I guess the core number is an important variable. Is there any variable in the kernel that is related to the core number limitation? For example, core <=1024?

The "uncore" error was a regression (only in gnr-6.6-v29.3, not anymore in gnr-6.6-v32.1), and it was fixed by the patches in gnr-6.60-v32.1. From the logs, the "vmap" error is there in gnr-6.6-v32.1 and gnr-6.6-v29.3. Maybe already there even earlier than gnr-6.6-v29.3, which need to be figured out. I have invited our team member Andrew Zaborowski  @Zaborowski, Andrew  to deep dive into the vmap issue.
Do we have existing Jira ticket that the Linux team is working on the vmap issue ?   @Zaborowski, Andrew @Pan, Lijun
We have https://jira.devtools.intel.com/browse/LINUXBKC3-537 but without progress yet.

From earlier comments it sounds like this is not a kernel bug (or at least, a kernel change hasn't tipped the memory usage over the limit).  So most likely the BKC userspace but we can't be sure.  Can we isolate the component by leaving the WW51 (or later) OS on these machines but reverting non-OS components to older version? This HSD had a similar signature but it has been long fixed: https://hsdes.intel.com/appstore/article/#/18024968291 and it started to happen at around 900 cores. An 8S-only issue likely means that some component is allocating memory per-core or thread, and at some number of cores there's no enough memory of that type.  We can try to find out which module fails to load but it doesn't matter, the memory hog is probably some other module or core kernel code that started before.  It may have reserved too much memory indefinitely but more likely just temporarily, so for example systemd-udevd may be unable to load some modules at that specific moment but it may retry the next second and succeed.  In the logs, after the stack trace more modules are successfully loaded so likely there's just a bottleneck moment.  So the low reproduction rate could be because of timing. Can I request access to one of the machines that are able to reproduce this?  First step would be to either reserve extra memory or set a lower limit with vmalloc= to make this easier to reproduce.  Then maybe try setting a breakpoint at warn_alloc() to force the OS stop and inspect where is all the kernel memory gone.

I will help enable a system with previous IFWI, but I strongly suspect the increase of the core number when we upgraded the CPU is the most relevant factor.

Ok, let's see if we can make progress quickly here, but this is a harmless error with no functional implications as far as I can tell. Jin Wang, thanks, I'm using that machine now, let me know when you need it back.  I was able to reproduce once (in 52 cycles) but my debug script didn't catch that moment on time so I'm trying again with some changes (at 200 cycles now).  I'm using kexec to boot more quickly but it's still rather slow. Even when the issue is not reproduced I see a spike in module loads around that time in boot, it lasts only for about 0.5s, reaching 1400 simultaneous allocations in __do_sys_init_module() of 3MB each, amounting to > 6GB usage.  They have the "vpages" flag in /proc/vmallocinfo, I have to check what that implies.  Since all the allocations are same size this suggest a single module is being loaded simultaneously for each CPU, but this shouldn't happen, it that was supposed to have been fixed in 6.5 kernels last year. I have to find which module that is, and what in the first place creates the memory limit.  vmalloc allocations can have different flags and I assume different total limits, yet there's much more RAM available so what causes the "vpages" areas to be limited?  vmalloc allocations in /proc/vmallocinfo without that flag go to over 15GB total without issues.

I have the root cause and I'm looking for a solution. The root cause is basically the same as in https://hsdes.intel.com/appstore/article/#/18024968291 and the reason that the upstream fix isn't working is that the duplicate module loading guard was only added in the finit_module() syscall but not in init_module().  But CentOS Stream 9's systemd-udevd uses kmod-libs-28 which (wrongly) only uses finit_module() for uncompressed kernel modules.  When it tries to load a compressed kernel module, and all of our modules are compressed, it falls back to init_module().  Newer kmod versions don't have this problem but 28 is the last version available in CS9. Possible fixes: * in init_module() in the kernel, hash the module contents and add similar checks as Linus has added to finit_module() in his patch.  The problem is that by the time init_module() is called, the contents have already been loaded and decompressed so the saving is smaller so I'm not sure such change would be accepted upstream. * build our own kmod-libs package based on newer sources, I'll talk to California Sullivan about this. * use a newer RPM from some other distro, unfortunately the ones I tries depended on newer glibc also. * uncompress our kernel modules above some size.  For example by setting the lower limit at 1MB these are only about 50 modules.  This would be an easy workaround, it can be applied with the following command:     find /lib/modules/6.6.0-* -type f -name '*.ko.xz' -size +100000c -exec unxz '{}' + ; depmod
Thanks  @Zaborowski, Andrew for working on the issue, do you still need the system? If your EB is available I can still help verify it.

Jin Wang, I don't need the system anymore.  If we have a kmod-libs package to test I can ask you again for access.  California Sullivan pointed out that since this issue is harmless the updated kmod-libs package may not be accepted by CCF so it may be not worth pursuing the fix.  Dongmin Wang, please comment. (sorry I can't add @ links) There's no kernel EB, the workaround is in userspace: find /lib/modules/6.6.0-* -type f -name '*.ko.xz' -size +100000c -exec unxz '{}' + ; depmod

comments_structured.author: azaborow
comments_structured.text: From earlier comments it sounds like this is not a kernel bug (or at least, a kernel change hasn't tipped the memory usage over the limit).  So most likely the BKC userspace but we can't be sure.  Can we isolate the component by leaving the WW51 (or later) OS on these machines but reverting non-OS components to older version? This HSD had a similar signature but it has been long fixed: https://hsdes.intel.com/appstore/article/#/18024968291 and it started to happen at around 900 cores. An 8S-only issue likely means that some component is allocating memory per-core or thread, and at some number of cores there's no enough memory of that type.  We can try to find out which module fails to load but it doesn't matter, the memory hog is probably some other module or core kernel code that started before.  It may have reserved too much memory indefinitely but more likely just temporarily, so for example systemd-udevd may be unable to load some modules at that specific moment but it may retry the next second and succeed.  In the logs, after the stack trace more modules are successfully loaded so likely there's just a bottleneck moment.  So the low reproduction rate could be because of timing. Can I request access to one of the machines that are able to reproduce this?  First step would be to either reserve extra memory or set a lower limit with vmalloc= to make this easier to reproduce.  Then maybe try setting a breakpoint at warn_alloc() to force the OS stop and inspect where is all the kernel memory gone.

Jin Wang, thanks, I'm using that machine now, let me know when you need it back.  I was able to reproduce once (in 52 cycles) but my debug script didn't catch that moment on time so I'm trying again with some changes (at 200 cycles now).  I'm using kexec to boot more quickly but it's still rather slow. Even when the issue is not reproduced I see a spike in module loads around that time in boot, it lasts only for about 0.5s, reaching 1400 simultaneous allocations in __do_sys_init_module() of 3MB each, amounting to > 6GB usage.  They have the "vpages" flag in /proc/vmallocinfo, I have to check what that implies.  Since all the allocations are same size this suggest a single module is being loaded simultaneously for each CPU, but this shouldn't happen, it that was supposed to have been fixed in 6.5 kernels last year. I have to find which module that is, and what in the first place creates the memory limit.  vmalloc allocations can have different flags and I assume different total limits, yet there's much more RAM available so what causes the "vpages" areas to be limited?  vmalloc allocations in /proc/vmallocinfo without that flag go to over 15GB total without issues.

comments_structured.author: azaborow
comments_structured.text: I have the root cause and I'm looking for a solution. The root cause is basically the same as in https://hsdes.intel.com/appstore/article/#/18024968291 and the reason that the upstream fix isn't working is that the duplicate module loading guard was only added in the finit_module() syscall but not in init_module().  But CentOS Stream 9's systemd-udevd uses kmod-libs-28 which (wrongly) only uses finit_module() for uncompressed kernel modules.  When it tries to load a compressed kernel module, and all of our modules are compressed, it falls back to init_module().  Newer kmod versions don't have this problem but 28 is the last version available in CS9. Possible fixes: * in init_module() in the kernel, hash the module contents and add similar checks as Linus has added to finit_module() in his patch.  The problem is that by the time init_module() is called, the contents have already been loaded and decompressed so the saving is smaller so I'm not sure such change would be accepted upstream. * build our own kmod-libs package based on newer sources, I'll talk to California Sullivan about this. * use a newer RPM from some other distro, unfortunately the ones I tries depended on newer glibc also. * uncompress our kernel modules above some size.  For example by setting the lower limit at 1MB these are only about 50 modules.  This would be an easy workaround, it can be applied with the following command:     find /lib/modules/6.6.0-* -type f -name '*.ko.xz' -size +100000c -exec unxz '{}' + ; depmod

The root cause is basically the same as in https://hsdes.intel.com/appstore/article/#/18024968291 and the reason that the upstream fix isn't working is that the duplicate module loading guard was only added in the finit_module() syscall but not in init_module().  But CentOS Stream 9's systemd-udevd uses kmod-libs-28 which (wrongly) only uses finit_module() for uncompressed kernel modules.  When it tries to load a compressed kernel module, and all of our modules are compressed, it falls back to init_module().  Newer kmod versions don't have this problem but 28 is the last version available in CS9. Possible fixes: * in init_module() in the kernel, hash the module contents and add similar checks as Linus has added to finit_module() in his patch.  The problem is that by the time init_module() is called, the contents have already been loaded and decompressed so the saving is smaller so I'm not sure such change would be accepted upstream. * build our own kmod-libs package based on newer sources, I'll talk to California Sullivan about this. * use a newer RPM from some other distro, unfortunately the ones I tries depended on newer glibc also. * uncompress our kernel modules above some size.  For example by setting the lower limit at 1MB these are only about 50 modules.  This would be an easy workaround, it can be applied with the following command:     find /lib/modules/6.6.0-* -type f -name '*.ko.xz' -size +100000c -exec unxz '{}' + ; depmod

Summary: GNR-AP: from ww35 to ww50, no UPI error hit (40+ system * 2000 cycles * 8 BKCs) GNR-SP: from ww37 to ww52, no UPI error hit (~40 system * 2000 cycles * 7 BKCs) Overall, the reproduce rate of UPI failure is very very low. We just hit once for each GNR AP/SP platform in PV validation.  @Nelson, Paul Please help to comment on whether it's our expectation for UPI error occurrence. Copy the conclusion for last UPI error occurrence here:  14613102515  ================================================ Bozic, Thomas Last updated on: Wednesday, September 18th 2024 5:15:57 am (4 months ago) id: 14613102515 Summary: Recommending 'rejected -> cannot_reproduce'; however, continuous monitoring for these errors is recommended, and should the error be reproducible, we will revisit this disposition accordingly. 1) extensive efforts to reproduce the failures were unsuccessful across all systems tested for days to weeks AND 2) the errors reported have been single bit errors AND 3) are categorized as a 'corrected' type , so there is no data corruption AND 4) electrical characterization is showing compliance with the UPI specification across all parts tested AND 5) outgoing DPM < 1 with 99.9% confidence Background: This HSD is discussing the occurrence of single bit errors, as indicated by the KTICRCERRCNT=0x1, that are of a 'corrected' error type. As the bit error was corrected by a subsequent replay of the transaction by the machine, there is no data corruption experienced by the customer. Reproduction: Extensive efforts have been made to reproduce the error across all systems, including the originally impacted systems and the entire Cluster fleet. These efforts have spanned several days to weeks, encompassing a wide range of operating conditions and stress tests. Despite these rigorous attempts, the error has not been successfully reproduced. The inability to replicate the error suggests that it is not a persistent or widespread issue, and it may be attributed to transient environmental factors or rare, unpredictable events that are not indicative of hardware defects. UPI Spec: The UPI (Ultra Path Interconnect) specification supports a raw - before CRC correction - bit error rate of 1E-12. Compliance to UPI Spec: It requires 3m12s of testing at 24gbps with 0 failures to achieve 99% confidence that the link has a BER < 1E-12. On previous data characterization for Recipe 20 stability, we have shown 0 failures across 15+ million BER spec trials, which implies a 99% confidence in < 1 DPM or parts having BER exceeding the UPI specification.

As the bit error was corrected by a subsequent replay of the transaction by the machine, there is no data corruption experienced by the customer. Reproduction: Extensive efforts have been made to reproduce the error across all systems, including the originally impacted systems and the entire Cluster fleet. These efforts have spanned several days to weeks, encompassing a wide range of operating conditions and stress tests. Despite these rigorous attempts, the error has not been successfully reproduced. The inability to replicate the error suggests that it is not a persistent or widespread issue, and it may be attributed to transient environmental factors or rare, unpredictable events that are not indicative of hardware defects. UPI Spec: The UPI (Ultra Path Interconnect) specification supports a raw - before CRC correction - bit error rate of 1E-12. Compliance to UPI Spec: It requires 3m12s of testing at 24gbps with 0 failures to achieve 99% confidence that the link has a BER < 1E-12. On previous data characterization for Recipe 20 stability, we have shown 0 failures across 15+ million BER spec trials, which implies a 99% confidence in < 1 DPM or parts having BER exceeding the UPI specification.

Do we know the expected failure rate for 8S? The current fail rate is around 3/22k, is it acceptable?  @Nelsen, Paul  Yes that is acceptable.  We do not publish an "expected error rate" because the target is 0 CRC errors.  However, we know that longer UPI cables are more susceptible to noise, and the open-chassis design is more susceptible to electrical interference. You can calculate the observed BER based on # of errors seen over time.  With 14 links of 24 lanes at 24Ghz, if you have 3 errors per hour (3600 seconds) that would be 3/(14*24*24G*3600) = 1.03E-16.  This is 4 orders of magnitude better than the spec allows (1E-12). Detail: - code 0x30 CRC errors are corrected with no side-effects.  We retry the FLIT until it succeeds.  Since you only see 1 error at a time, the retry appears to be succeeding on the immediate next try. - code 0x31 CRC with reset means there was a burst of CRC errors (reflected in KTICRCERR register) and the link was reset to try to clear up the errors.   - you can try lowering the speed from 24Ghz to 16Ghz and see if that reduces the error rate, and decide if the performance is more important, or having 0 CRC errors is more important. - 0 CRC errors was achieved in the 2S cluster with 400+ systems running, but that was 6 months ago.  You can check with them, if they have measured the error rate over the last 6 months.   (the 8S system has 14+ links, so it should see ~2.5x error rate compared to 2S)
Thanks Paul. Can I calculate like this? On average each cycle takes around 960 s for 8S. The total time for 22k cycles is 960*22,000s So the failure rate is: 3/(14*24*24G*960*22,000) = 1.76E-21 < 1E-12 Is the 24G applicable for cycling condition?
The issue happens when the system is about to enter the OS, the UPI enters and exits L0p at that time. The calculation result is 9 orders of magnitude better than the spec allows. Even if we use a bandwidth far less than 24Ghz, the failure rate is still better than the spec definition.  Reject this HSD as won't fix.

You can calculate the observed BER based on # of errors seen over time.  With 14 links of 24 lanes at 24Ghz, if you have 3 errors per hour (3600 seconds) that would be 3/(14*24*24G*3600) = 1.03E-16.  This is 4 orders of magnitude better than the spec allows (1E-12). Detail: - code 0x30 CRC errors are corrected with no side-effects.  We retry the FLIT until it succeeds.  Since you only see 1 error at a time, the retry appears to be succeeding on the immediate next try. - code 0x31 CRC with reset means there was a burst of CRC errors (reflected in KTICRCERR register) and the link was reset to try to clear up the errors.   - you can try lowering the speed from 24Ghz to 16Ghz and see if that reduces the error rate, and decide if the performance is more important, or having 0 CRC errors is more important. - 0 CRC errors was achieved in the 2S cluster with 400+ systems running, but that was 6 months ago.  You can check with them, if they have measured the error rate over the last 6 months.   (the 8S system has 14+ links, so it should see ~2.5x error rate compared to 2S)

Hi  @Wang, Jin1  no, this doesn't seem to be the same with 061 HSD. The delta between 24.40 and 24.51 is quite big, my EB did not contain some or most of the changes I see in change log.  I remember we debugged node-manager out of memory issue and it was abandoned due to low repro rate. Is repro rate higher now? Does disabling node-manager restart helps: https://hsdes.intel.com/appstore/article/#/1862117293 ? I also see many peci_cmds instances in process list which might be expected in case CPUs sending NEED_RETRY response code via peci-wire so that the queue is quite big.  But it should have gone bigger than previously if this is the root cause. Has the host boot time increased? Can we check CPU response code via peci-wire after host booted?  There are couple of PECI-related changes in crashdump: https://github.com/intel-collab/firmware.bmc.openbmc.applications.crashdump/pull/545 and ras-manager: https://github.com/intel-collab/firmware.bmc.openbmc.applications.ras-manager/pull/578 Owners should evaluate whether this change take into account the CPU bug with sending NEED_RETRY code during boot and what is the possible impact.

Hi  @Shulzhenko, Oleksandr , from my data, the reproduction rate is around 1/200. I can disable node-manager to have a try The boot time remains unchanged, we did not change IFWI this week, just changing bmc and cpld then see the issue

Hi @Wang, Jin1 I got it. So my suggestion remains the same:  1) Evaluate with NM team why VM consumption greatly increased; 2) Evaluate with the owners two pull requests I mentioned (especially one from the crashdump). I suspect that the reason is that we have more peci-wire requests queued than usual and this is the reason NM consumes more memory than previously and thus we have more frequent OOM crash.

Relating to Crashdump: I looked in the serial logs provided and I don’t see crashdump using a lot of memory, nor do I see an indication that there is an IERR/MCERR Event and/or any indication that crashdump is currently running.   However, based off mem available being around 50M, another problem is that if crashdump runs at all here, it may very well crash the system,! !!! Why’s it so low? It does look like Node manager has a lot of mem… (If I’m reading that right. )   Regarding this change: https://github.com/intel-collab/firmware.bmc.openbmc.applications.crashdump/pull/545   I’m not sure if this is involved at all here, but let me explain what this change does..   This change was meant to solve a problem where upon crashdump start up that there’s NO CPU’s detected, This fix is that it will continually  execute PECI “PING”,  to determine when CPU’s are available and then continue with initialization.   So, I see 2 scenarios: CPU is Powered off. PECI “PING” returning bad CC value.   In these cases, (and only on Crashdump start) Crashdump will check for CPU’s with “PECI Ping”  if we don’t find at least 1 CPU, Wait 10 s, and try again.. and it will do that infinitely. Until success.   However, I’m not quite seeing how this would cause a memory usage issue.   To eliminate crashdump as the out of memory culprit, can you turn off the crashdump service? From what I can see, it should still fail with the out of memory issue.

Some updates from my side 1.Disabling the node manager and the system run pretty well so far, but I checked the previous bmc version 24.40 and its node-manager memory utilization is also around 380%~ 2. I will revert back my script first to confirm it is not caused by my script's change. Target is reaching 200 cycle each system 3. comments_structured.text: Relating to Crashdump: I looked in the serial logs provided and I don’t see crashdump using a lot of memory, nor do I see an indication that there is an IERR/MCERR Event and/or any indication that crashdump is currently running.   However, based off mem available being around 50M, another problem is that if crashdump runs at all here, it may very well crash the system,! !!! Why’s it so low? It does look like Node manager has a lot of mem… (If I’m reading that right. )   Regarding this change: https://github.com/intel-collab/firmware.bmc.openbmc.applications.crashdump/pull/545   I’m not sure if this is involved at all here, but let me explain what this change does..   This change was meant to solve a problem where upon crashdump start up that there’s NO CPU’s detected, This fix is that it will continually  execute PECI “PING”,  to determine when CPU’s are available and then continue with initialization.   So, I see 2 scenarios: CPU is Powered off. PECI “PING” returning bad CC value.   In these cases, (and only on Crashdump start) Crashdump will check for CPU’s with “PECI Ping”  if we don’t find at least 1 CPU, Wait 10 s, and try again.. and it will do that infinitely. Until success.   However, I’m not quite seeing how this would cause a memory usage issue.   To eliminate crashdump as the out of memory culprit, can you turn off the crashdump service? From what I can see, it should still fail with the out of memory issue.
